rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At the Qur’an’s revelation and Gabriel’s advent, the heavens were specially protected against infiltration.
rows.anchor: in the time of revelation of the Qur’ ān and at advent of Gabriel also the heavens had been put under special protection

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The jinn’s testimony refutes the idolaters’ charge that the Qur’an was soothsaying like discourse inspired by jinn; their observation alone sufficed.
rows.anchor: The Qur’ān has cited this information given by the jinn before the idolaters of Arabia

rows.speaker: the jinn
rows.claim: They did not know the cause of the cosmic change and only guessed it heralded a great revolution on earth, unsure whether it would help its inhabitants.
rows.anchor: These jinn were not absolutely sure about the reason behind this great change in the universe

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passive wording for possible harm and active wording for good imply the jinn leaned toward the change benefiting earth’s inhabitants; they linked it with Qur’anic revelation as two auspicious events.
rows.anchor: mentioned that something ill may befall them in the passive voice and mentioned that something good will befall them in the active voice

rows.speaker: the jinn
rows.claim: The jinn say their paths differ, although they had not yet distinguished good from evil; the Qur’an clarifies that their ways are separate.
rows.anchor: the Qur’ān cleared this misconception of theirs and clarified that all of them do not follow the same path

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Association and disassociation should rest on belief and disbelief rather than tribal or national allegiance.
rows.anchor: the basis of association and dissociation should be belief and disbelief. It should not be

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The jinn’s statement disavows a nation that persisted in disbelief and polytheism despite their call to faith; prophets and the righteous likewise disavow unbelieving peoples, as did the Companions of the Cave.
rows.anchor: declaration of acquittal from their nation, which, even after their calls to accept faith, remained adamant on its disbelief and polytheism

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word for paths also means schools of thought.
rows.anchor: means “paths” and “schools of thought”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After calling their people to truth, the jinn warn that they remain in God’s grasp and cannot escape Him on earth or in heaven.
rows.anchor: they are always in the grasp of God; He can seize them at any time

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Parallelism suppresses paired words in the verse: “earth” implies an omitted counterpart in the second clause, and “fleeing” implies one in the first; the translation unfolds them because the elliptical style is unfamiliar in Urdu.
rows.anchor: some words are suppressed on the basis of the well-known linguistic principle of parallelism

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The jinn model accepting guidance when it reaches them: truth must be recognized, while evasion exposes a choice of desire over reason.
rows.anchor: mandatory upon them to recognize the truth and so they professed faith in it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bakhs means to reduce.
rows.anchor: means “ to reduce” and the word

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rahq means unfairness; 20:112 parallels this wording by saying believers need fear neither wrong nor injustice.
rows.anchor: explained earlier, means “to be unfair.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The jinn reassure new believers that faith brings no loss: God rewards deeds abundantly, usurps no right, and wrongs no one; every small good or evil deed will be seen (99:7–8).
rows.anchor: whoever will do so should rest assured that this deal will procure no loss

rows.speaker: the jinn
rows.claim: The jinn say some among them are obedient and others disobedient; those obedient are rightly guided and the disobedient become fuel for Hell.
rows.anchor: those who are obedient will find themselves on the right path and those who are disobedient will become the firewood of Hell

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Innate moral awareness, revelation, and the observed difference between obedient and disobedient jinn require God’s just distinction between them; treating good and evil alike would make creation purposeless.
rows.anchor: a natural consequence of all this is that the Almighty should not regard both these categories to be equal

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The discourse now turns from the jinn’s testimony directly to Quraysh; the opening “Say” had directed the Prophet to convey their view of the Qur’an and its message.
rows.anchor: After the impressions and statements of the jinn, from here the discourse has shifted directly towards the Quraysh.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For Quraysh, steadfastness on tawḥīd would be profitable in this life and the next, and God would grant them abundant rain.
rows.anchor: if they had remained steadfast on the straight path, then this would not have been a loss-incurring deed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Abundant water” connotes plentiful resources and provision (compare 71:10–12); Quraysh wrongly credited their wealth and children to idols and feared faith would take them away, though all favors come from God and gratitude brings their preservation and increase.
rows.anchor: connotes abundance in resources and provisions. Examples of this usage can be seen in the previous sūrahs.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The straight path means tawḥīd, a reality recognized by human nature and intellect and taught by God’s prophets and Books.
rows.anchor: It is a reality and hence human nature bears witness to it, human intellect alludes to it and the prophets and books of God have also called people towards this path.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worldly riches are a test of gratitude and obedience, not proof that their recipients are God’s favorites; Quraysh’s leaders mistook inherited privilege for a right and arrogantly rejected the Reminder.
rows.anchor: the real purpose for this bestowal is to test that person, whether he becomes grateful and obedient to the Almighty after receiving these favours

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The words “and whoever” introduce a second warning: those who proudly turn away from their Lord’s Reminder will face ever-increasing torment.
rows.anchor: sound a second admonition to the leaders of the Quraysh that those who evade the reminder of their Lord

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although commonly rendered “extreme torment,” ṣaʿadan means “to increase”; punishment for rejecting God’s prophet and Book is therefore lasting and ever-growing, greater in the Hereafter than in this world.
rows.anchor: I am inclined to think that the punishment of those whom the Almighty seizes because of the rejection of His prophet and Book is not transient; it is ever-increasing.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Reminder from which Quraysh turns away is the Qur’an, whose rejection was condemned earlier.
rows.anchor: refers to the Qur’ ān on the lack of recognition of which the Quraysh have been condemned earlier

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The direct warning to Quraysh recalls tawḥīd: since God alone can be worshipped, alleged deities cannot rescue them, and they must not pollute the mosque by worshipping them.
rows.anchor: the Quraysh are directly addressed and warned of the sanctity a mosque has in which no one but God is worshipped

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mosques are reserved for God by their very purpose: neither may one be built for another nor may anyone else be worshipped there.
rows.anchor: Neither can a mosque be built for someone other than God nor can someone other than Him be worshipped in it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though unspecified, “mosques” likely refers to the Baytullāh because Quraysh are addressed; the plural marks it as the direction joining all mosques and also states a general rule, as in 9:17.
rows.anchor: there is a strong indication that it refers to the Baytull āh. It is signified by a plural word

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Libadan is the plural of libdah, meaning intertwined or multilayered; it depicts tawḥīd as alien in the very house built for worship of the one God, where opponents crowd the Prophet during prayer and preaching to harass him.
rows.anchor: which means something which is intertwined or something which is multi-layered.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAbd Allāh refers to the Prophet; the affectionate expression also presents invoking God alone as a servant’s most natural and logical course, though some consciences recoil from it.
rows.anchor: refers to the Prophet (sws). The expression reflects affection

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Despite his opponents’ disgust, the Prophet must declare that he invokes God alone and ascribes no partners to Him, even when they assign those partners a share with God.
rows.anchor: he will invoke God alone and not ascribe partners to Him, even though they might regard these partners to have a great share

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet cannot compel unwilling opponents or control their harm, benefit, guidance, or misguidance; he was sent to invite them to truth and deliver God’s word, with no further obligation.
rows.anchor: he has been sent as one who invites people to the truth and not one who makes them forcibly accept it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur’anic parallelism suppresses the counterpart to “harm” and the counterpart to “right guidance” in this verse.
rows.anchor: the unique style of the Qur’ ān may be noted that because of parallelism

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet must say that associating anyone with God to appease or fear his opponents would falsely attribute the gravest crime to God, for which no one can shelter him from divine punishment.
rows.anchor: this would be imputing falsehood to God which is the greatest crime.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The crime of associating partners with God brings punishment from which no one can provide refuge or asylum.
rows.anchor: no one will be able to give him refuge and asylum from the wrath of God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This continues verse 21: the Prophet cannot bring the punishment at their demand or force guidance; his sole duty is to transmit God’s message faithfully and give the full directives.
rows.anchor: his responsibility is only to communicate the message of God with full integrity of contents

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Risālātihi is tied to balāghan to stress that the Prophet must communicate God’s message exactly, cannot guide or misguide independently, and may not alter a directive to please opponents.
rows.anchor: the purpose of addition of this word is to show that the responsibility of the Prophet (sws) is only to communicate the message of God in its exact form

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After fulfilling that communication, the Prophet has discharged his obligation; those who still disobey God and His Messenger face eternal Hell.
rows.anchor: After this, those who remain adamant in disobeying God and His Prophet (sws) should remember that for them is the fire of Hell

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The proud opponents will learn who is truly weak when they see the threatened punishment, which includes both the rejecters’ worldly punishment and the Hereafter; 71:25 treats the same matter.
rows.anchor: when they will see the promised punishment, they will realize whether it is they who are frail and weak or the Prophet of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Opponents pressed the Prophet to hasten the punishment and ask its time; he must say he does not know whether it is imminent or God will defer it.
rows.anchor: The opponents of the Prophet (sws) wanted to hasten the punishment which he was promising them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promised punishment may be imminent or deferred by God, but its exact timing is unknown to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: the exact time of its arrival is not known to him; it could be imminent and it could have been deferred by the Almighty.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God alone knows the unseen facts whose knowledge rests exclusively with Him, such as the time of punishment in the Hereafter; He does not disclose them even to angels or prophets.
rows.anchor: it refers to those facts whose knowledge rests only with Him. For example, the time of the punishment of the Hereafter is only known to Him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God need not disclose every unseen fact to a messenger, since the messenger can fulfill his office without knowing them all; God guards His messengers to ensure faithful delivery.
rows.anchor: it is not necessary that the Almighty inform his prophets whom He selects for this position of all the facts of the unknown world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception is a severed exception, independent of the preceding clause and explained by the following enunciative; the author compares it with 88:21–24.
rows.anchor: In technical terms, such an exception is called the severed exception ( istithnā munqaṭa‘); it is independent of the previous clause

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording also occurs with the same sense in 47:31 and 10:14: although God knows everything, He tests people so their inner selves become manifest.
rows.anchor: The Almighty has knowledge of all things; however, He wants the inner-self of a person to be revealed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God protects the revelations entrusted to His prophets, surrounds them, and counts everything He gives them, down to the smallest thing.
rows.anchor: revelations He entrusts to His prophets and keeps count of every single thing He gives them. The smallest of things cannot escape this count.
